Mycenae. A fortress city in the Peloponnese was the dominant political and military power of the Late Bronze Age, spanning from 1600 to 1100 BCE, and served as the legendary seat of Agamemnon. Its imposing Lion Gate, massive stone walls, and chamber tombs reveal a highly organized civilization that dominated the eastern Mediterranean before declining mysteriously around 1100 BCE.

Mycenae was ruled by Agamemnon, the leader of the Greek forces in the Trojan War according to Homer and later tradition, making it the symbolic capital of the Greeks at Troy. The city featured the famous Lion Gate, a monumental entrance with two lions rampant flanking the doorway, a symbol of Mycenaean power and architectural achievement. The walls were built with Cyclopean masonry—massive, roughly-hewn stone blocks fitted together without mortar—which suggested to later Greeks that only divine or superhuman forces could have constructed them.

Within the city stood the Treasury of Atreus, also called the Tomb of Agamemnon, a tholos tomb of extraordinary engineering. It featured a corbelled vault covering a vast underground chamber. Mycenae headed the Mycenaean civilization, a Bronze Age culture from 1600 to 1100 BCE that unified the Greek mainland, established trade networks, and influenced the entire Aegean world.

The city fell around 1100 BCE amid the Bronze Age Collapse, a mysterious period of widespread destruction and upheaval that swept across the Mediterranean, ending Bronze Age civilizations. Mycenae was rediscovered by archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann in the 1870s. Schliemann excavated shaft graves and proclaimed he had found the tomb of Agamemnon himself, though this claim has been questioned by later scholars.

Agamemnon was the legendary king of Mycenae who led the Trojan War. Helen of Troy, the daughter of King Tyndareus, was his relation—her abduction sparked the Trojan War that Agamemnon commanded from Mycenae. Homer immortalized Mycenaean civilization in the Iliad and Odyssey.
